utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today we'll start to hear the evidence through videolink. Is the videolink functioning well? Madam Registrar, at the other side of the videolink, could I ask you whether you hear me, whether you see me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. We can hear you and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we can hear you and we can see you as well, which means that there are no technical obstacles and we'll start. Could the witness please stand. Good morning, Mr. Deuric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you inform us about who are present in the room at the other side of the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, apart from the witness and myself, there is an IT official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. I think you'll see him soon on your screen. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you kindly tell us your full name and surname slowly.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I am Momir Deuric, son of Lazo, born on 5 July 1946 in Vlasenica municipality, the settlement of Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, did you at one point in time give a written statement to the Defence team of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we call up in e-court 65 ter 1D04305. Could we please look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, do you see this before you now?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the signature on this page, as well as the date, written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, having made a solemn declaration in this courtroom, and after the proofing we conducted before you appeared in the courtroom, would your answers to the same questions be the same as in the statement and would you confirm still today that this statement reflects the best of your recollection and knowledge about the events you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, my statement is entirely true, and I have nothing to change in it. All of it is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender the statement of Witness Momir Deuric, which is 65 ter 1D04305.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D04305 receives number D797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave, Your Honours, I should like to read the summary of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, Momir Deuric, found himself in his workplace at the staff of the TO of Vlasenica when the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was responsible for the security of the TO depot at an installation in Susica settlement in Vlasenica. There were another four colleagues, two Muslims and two Serbs, doing the same job. The witness eye-witnessed the pre-war national homogenisation disputes between different ethnic groups around the future of Yugoslavia, the response to mobilisation, and the arming of people of both Serb and Muslim ethnicity. As the war came nearer and nearer to Vlasenica, people were seized by panic which caused massive movements of Serbs towards Serbia and Muslims towards Kladanj and Tuzla. The ethnic groups in urban and rural environments alike were afraid of each other which resulted in general mistrust. After 21st April 1992 and the proclamation of general mobilisation, the witness received a war-time assignment to continue securing the Susica installation. He was an eye-witness when, in early May 1992, Serb populus that had fled their homes and found refuge in Vlasenica from the areas of Gorazde, Kladanj, and Olovo started arriving. They were put up in one part of the depot in Susica which did not hold any military equipment. This Serb populus gradually left this installation, finding better accommodation. Later on, that facility was taken over by the army which started bringing in Muslims allegedly from Memici village and later from Vlasenica as well. There were cases when Muslim families came of their own accord to spend the night there, pending further transportation because they didn't feel safe at home. During his stay and work at Susica, the witness saw on several occasions some foreign delegations visiting, escorted by the police, and later found out that they were representatives of the International Red Cross. On 26th September 1992, after the attack of Muslim forces at Rogosija village and after some of the members of his extended family were killed, he was militarily engaged. After a couple of days, when he met with Dragan Nikolic, he found out from Dragan Nikolic that, in the meantime, the admission centre of Susica had been closed down and the persons who had been there were taken for an exchange. Your Honours, this is a short summary of this witness's statement, and if you don't mind, I would like to ask only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do as you suggest, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, I will put to you only a couple of questions about things you may know about the food provided to people who were put up there while you were working at the admission centre of Susica. Where was the food provided from; and what was it like?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: They received food from Vlasenica. I don't know exactly which kitchen prepared it, but I believe it was called Putnik. Food was excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When going about your duty as security for part of the Susica installation which held military equipment, did you receive the same food as the people who were housed in Susica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same food.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the facility you were securing, were you physically separated from the facility where they were put up?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Those were two facilities, two buildings. One of them stored military equipment, and I spent most of my time in that building. I rearranged and re-stacked the equipment because when they would come, they would draw some supplies and leave it in disorder, and then I had to put some order into it again. It was a separate building from the one where the rest of the people were put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After being recruited, after the well-known events in Rogosija village, did you ever come back to the Susica facility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994. Until then I was at the front line, and then they assigned me to go back to my old workplace at the depot. It was sometime in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, until the end of the war, were there prisoners at any time in the Susica facility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: There were no prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, thank you for your answers. You will now be probably examined by my learned friends from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deuric.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll be asking you questions mainly about Susica camp. But before I do that, I'd like to take you to paragraph 26 of your statement. You say you participated in combat operations at Cerska and Kravica in March 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you speak about an incident involving Muslim fighters on Mount Udrc and you say they came down from that mountain and killed 12 soldiers from the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is a combat report of 2nd March 1993. It's from the command of the Zvornik Brigade to the command of the Drina Corps, and it speaks about that area at that time. I'd like to take you to the second half of point 1. The text reads: "At around 8.30 hours, columns of civilians and soldiers with pack animals were noticed from Udrc and Rasevo towards Konjevic Polje. The columns were hit with every available means." So near the same place you speak about these Muslims killing 12 soldiers in the 1st Krajina Corps, and at the same time as that incident, the VRS was shelling columns that included civilians with all available means; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: That is not true. From Udrc, that group came out and killed 12 soldiers of the Krajina Corps. In Cerska we didn't find any civilians. This group had been on mountain Udrc and they came down to the nearest village, Babici, because the Krajina Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, I'm asking you about this report which is a separate incident, albeit at the same place at the same time, about the VRS shelling columns that included civilians and hitting them with all available means that they had. Are you aware of that happening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. We passed through Cerska going to Konjevic Polje, and from Konjevic Polje to Kravica, we didn't see any civilians on our way. I'm talking about myself and my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I understand from my colleague that is, in fact, already admitted as P06928. My thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, in your own operations at this time, you were co-ordinating with the 1st Krajina Corps and a special unit commanded by Commander Mauzer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know who commanded that unit. Our unit was from Vlasenica, and it passed through Cerska, Konjevic Polje, on our way to Kravica. On the left and on the right, I don't know which units were there. And when we left Kravica and came to Siljkovici village, then we saw that we had the 1st Krajina Corps to our right. We stayed for about four or five days there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 09775. This is a Drina Corps combat order from the 12th of February, 1993. I'd like to move to page 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S. And I'm looking for paragraph 5.3. And here we see the Bratunac lpbr with a battalion of the 1st Krajina Corps and the 3rd Infantry Battalion are to mount an attack. They are to carry out active operations with a special operations brigade where Mauzer is in command. You were part of the 3rd Infantry Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Kravica was the area that you were deployed in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your objective was to capture Kravica village at that time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we were not involved in any combat. We advanced mostly in a column. We didn't see any civilians or enemy troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution would move to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 09775 receives number P6935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, could I ask you one additional question. In your previous answers, it -- you gave the impression that it was coincidence or at least that you found out only during the operations at the end that the Krajina Corps was there, I think you said, to your left. Do you have any knowledge about whether there was a co-ordination as is suggested by the document just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Krajina Corps was to our right, to the right of my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake, but -- whether they were to your right or to your left. But do you know anything about co-ordination between your unit and units from the Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, I'd like to turn to Susica camp now. You were working in a warehouse guarding TO material. How far away was the warehouse in which the prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Maybe 20 metres, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying there were no physical barriers within the camp, nothing stopping you walking from your warehouse to that warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Only the entrances were a bit further away, the entrance into both buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry if my question wasn't clear. I would just like you to confirm there was no physical barrier between the door of your warehouse and the door of the warehouse in which the prisoners were kept. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No, no. No barriers, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: There was an electricity pole in the shape of an A at the camp, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: How far away was that pole from the warehouse in which you were working?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly 20 metres away, 15, 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if I come out of the warehouse that you're working in, there is no obstacle between myself and the pole, no physical obstacle, is there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just for clarity on the record I'll rephrase that question. Is there any physical obstacle between the door of the warehouse in which you were working and the pole we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, several times empty boxes were piled up, those that had contained shells ammunition, et cetera, so that was between the door and the pole, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move on. You reported to Vlasenica Territorial Defence on 21st April 1992 in response to a summons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When you were providing security at the Territorial Defence facilities, you've said the army took over control of Susica at the end of May. Slobodan Pajic was a VRS officer who was present at Susica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Slobodan? I don't know which Slobodan this may be. There was Slobodan Pajic, but he wasn't in Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if I can take to your Karadzic testimony, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That is 65 ter number 31641. And I'd like to move to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: There is no B/C/S translation of this, sir, so I'm just going to read it out to you. You were being asked by a lawyer and he states the following: "After the same page this witness refers to Veljko Basic and Slobodan Pajic, who, according to this witness, took a bus load of women and children out of Susica and they were never returned. You told us about Veljko Basic in your statement. Slobodan Pajic was a VRS officer --" You say: "Yes." And then the question is repeated: "Slobodan Pajic was a VRS officer who was present at Susica, isn't it?" You answer: "Yes." You state that Veljko Basic was the camp warden, and then you move on. So, sir, if I can ask you again, Slobodan Pajic was a VRS officer who was present at Susica, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan was there briefly, though. He left Susica. I don't know where he went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When was he there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: In the month of May. I don't know ... I don't know exactly. End of May, I think. Mid-may, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Are you aware about -- that he carried out or ordered the carrying out of an assessment on security of Susica that was completed in June?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a moment. Who was your superior at Susica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I heard that Veljko was the warden of the camp. Veljko Bosic, a retired policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, you say that in your statement. Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: To us? Well, the late Bosko Nastic. He was later our company commander and the former Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank for that. Have I understood you correctly that Bosko Nastic was your superior when you were working at Susica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was Chief of Staff until 1991, and then he was replaced by Fikret Hodzic. No, Ferid Hodzic actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When was he replaced by Ferid Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: 1991. I don't know the month exactly. I think August, September, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And when the army took over the camp in May of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, matters become a bit confused, it seems. Witness, you were asked about Mr. Bosko Nastic. You were asked whether he was your superior when you were working at Susica. Was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, because he knew that warehouse, the equipment, and all of this where I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 21st of April, when I was assigned to Susica. And before the military operations, I worked in Susica too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 21st of April of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He then, in April 1992 -- who -- he was your superior, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And until when did he remain your superior in Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A month, I think, and then he went to the front. He was company commander there. As for the rest who worked in the Crisis Staff then, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I've received answers to my questions. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Prisoners of war were being held in Susica camp, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I think the interpreters can't hear you, sir. I wonder if you could try moving closer to the microphone. I'll repeat my question with a bit more clarity. Prisoners of war were being held in Susica camp after the army took over at the end of May 1992, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the month of May. I don't know exactly when the army took over, but it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And there were hundreds of detainees in Susica at any one time, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, when there were a lot of them there, then they would be sent for an exchange. As far as I know, people were exchanged as soon as there would be a lot of people there, especially civilians, women, children. They would send them off straight away. They would send them off straight away, when people wanted to go to Kladanj, Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, you use in your question, the term "prisoners of war." Did you intend to use that in a technical sense? Is it the position of the Prosecution that these were combatants taken prisoner or was it -- did you have something else on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm just about to challenge that term, if I can, using other evidence with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you're putting it to the witness that there were prisoners of war and then the witness says "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm about to bring up the fact that civilians were also held there with evidence to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move on to what you just said at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In fact, Susica camp was also holding women, children, and elderly as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned that there were some people who volunteered there because it was safer to be there than at home. That's what they would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, to be clear, the position of the Prosecution is that the army brought in civilians and held them at Susica and that included men who were not combatants, women, children, and elderly. And the Chamber has heard evidence from different witnesses as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of reference, I would reference RM088, P524, page 8, paragraph 36. And that witness mentions young women and girls. Other witnesses also mention civilians, including a pregnant woman and a disabled man being held for some time at Susica. I'm happy to provide the references to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, if you'd look at the answers, especially page 15, lines 12, 13, 14, the witness said that there were civilians, women and children. So at the same time, if you look at his answer - let me just check what line it is - about their status there, let me say it in that way, it seems that that's more the problem at least ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at page 16, the beginning of line 7, that's the second line in his answer, then it seems that if there's any dispute, it might be there rather than whether there were civilians. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, some detainees were held for lengthy periods of time at Susica camp. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but they went and did different kinds of work. They volunteered to work. Most of them were craftsmen anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, there was a visit from the CSCE on the 2nd of September, 1992, and they reported upon seeing the detainees that they appeared to be haggard, pale, and thin. And they concluded: "There can be little doubt that most are hungry." The detainees you saw at Susica camp, were they -- they were haggard, pale, and thin, were they not, at the start of September?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? Of course, there were those who were skinny by nature, who arrived there skinny, but even they volunteered to go and do different kinds of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 07021A. This is an excerpt from the report I've just mentioned. If we could have the second page in the English, please, and the second page in the B/C/S. The first page, Your Honours, is the cover page of the entire report and the rest is the excerpt. Under the heading: "Number of detainees and description," the second line -- my apologies. If we could have page 2 in the English. I'm getting ahead of myself. The heading is: "Health-related conditions" -- sorry, page 3 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The second paragraph under that heading, the third line in, it states: "Detainees appeared to be haggard, pale, and thin, but we were less able to assess the state of nourishment as they were dressed in heavier clothing. There can be little doubt that most are hungry." Now, Mr. Deuric, it is the position of the Prosecution that these detainees became this way because they were held in Susica for lengthy periods of time and not fed correctly.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. I know that food was brought in regularly and I know that everybody received food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we go back to page 2 in the English, same page of B/C/S, and now look at: "Number of detainees and description."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The second line reads: "We were told that this centre is used to hold and document prisoners as well as Serbian refugees for periods of several days, but we determined that at least several of these detainees have been held here for two months or more. It is our impression that these are innocent civilians who have not borne arms against the Serbian captors and that several of them were local residents." Firstly, Mr. Deuric, you would agree at least several of the detainees had been held there for two months or more?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know when people were brought in exactly or when they were taken out for exchanges or how long they were kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, earlier you were happy to tell the Court that some detainees arrived and were taken away straight away. That is the claim you made. If you knew about that, sir, you must have known several of the detainees were held for longer periods, including two months or more?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second, please, Witness. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered this question; namely, that he did not know how long these people were kept there, specifically two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With the introduction as given by Mr. MacDonald, the question is admissible. The witness may answer the question. Could you please answer the question. Mr. MacDonald asked you that -- why you were able to tell us that -- that some prisoners had left very quickly upon their arrival. Why wouldn't you know that others may not have left that quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please, as far as I know, some asked to be exchanged straight away. And others stayed, they wanted to work. They went out and did different kinds of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you personally meet with the Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, the ones I knew. There were quite a few of them that I knew and we would meet up and socialise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'm asking you this because, in paragraph 20 of your statement, I read: "Even while I was in Susica during the day, I would mainly spend the time in our premises to avoid being seen by Muslims whom I knew because they might have asked me for something." So there you say that you were more or less avoiding contact with the Muslims, whereas you tell me now that you would socialise with them. Could you please explain to me the variation in these answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, I could not avoid contact when they were ten people who all of them knew me. I didn't avoid contact. If they asked me to fetch something or to give them a cigarette or to light their cigarette, of course, we had contact. I didn't particularly avoid them. But I avoided situations in which they might ask for some kind of help I would be unable to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of help you thought they would ask from you, that you wanted to stay away from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of help? For instance, a man I knew, a friend of mine, asked me several times to take him somewhere to have a bath, and I was not allowed to do that. I just wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, if I could only remember. It was 22 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a friend of you, you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that you remember that a friend of yours asked you several times to take him somewhere to have a bath, and at the same time, you're telling us that you do not know who he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot the names of those people. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you know that he was a friend of yours. You know exactly what he asked you. You know that he was a soldier. But you don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the names. I knew them from military drills before the war. They would come before the war for military exercises. We got along well, but even then I didn't know the names of them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there were vague acquaintances rather than friends of yours. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Acquaintances. I knew them. All the men who had been at those military drills, they knew me by name, but when 100 of them would come for a military drill, I couldn't know everyone's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were not allowed to leave the camp, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. That was not my job. I spent my time in the depot where I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they had their own guards and commanders. Whether they allowed them to go out or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, otherwise he would have gone out and taken a bath wherever he wanted to take that bath, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because you are telling us that you knew that you couldn't take him anywhere where he could take a bath, that it was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not allowed for me. I had no authority over them. I had no authority to contact them. And I didn't have time. I was working at that depot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think -- do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wife and children were in Serbia. I was thinking in the evening I have time to go back home to feed the cattle and then come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you didn't have the time. But do you think that he would have repeatedly asked you to take him to a place where he could take a bath if he could have gone there himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought if I do that favour for one person, others would ask for it too, and I would have no time for all of them, and that's why I didn't want to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're contradicting yourself here to the extent that you say that you were not allowed to do it; whereas you now tell us you didn't do it because you wouldn't have time for all to do the same. Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't have permission, but even if I had permission, I couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, would it not just be the case that they were detained there and that they were prisoners and not allowed to go out and that you didn't take them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how and whether you understand it. I did not have time, nor did I ever ask my superiors if I was allowed to do it. And even if somebody had expressly allowed me, I couldn't do it because if I did it once, then I would be spending all my time doing only that and I would have no time left over for my own job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my question was a different one. Isn't it true that these people were not there volunteering in any way in either being there or doing their job because they were just prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Please proceed. I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have looked at the clock ten minutes earlier as a matter of fact. Apologies for that, for taking too long. Could the witness -- no, we don't have to ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom because he isn't in. We take a break, Witness, and we'll resume at 11.00. We'd like to see you back then. Mr. MacDonald -- oh, you're just standing. Yes. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I see, the videolink is still functioning. Is the audio okay as well? I'm asking Madam Registrar at the other side of the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours, we can hear you and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same is true for us. Mr. MacDonald, would you please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, with the last document we looked at, that was the CSCE mission to Susica at the start of September 1992, I read that their impression was that the people they spoke to that they determined had been there for two months or more were innocent civilians who had not borne arms against the Serbian captors. That impression is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will apologise if I misunderstood, but the Prosecution's question reads that, according to the report of the mission, those were civilians who were unarmed; whereas in the document before us in B/C/S it reads: "We had the impression that those were innocent civilians who did not attack the Serbs armed with weapons," which is not the same as not carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there's any mistake in the translation. I cannot verify that. But then it's an inappropriate way to deal with the matter, Mr. Stojanovic, because the -- Mr. Lukic is sitting next to you. I think Mr. MacDonald has just quoted the content of the report. And, therefore, unless there's any translation issue which should be dealt with in a different way, that is to seek verification of the translation rather than to comment on it. Witness, the impression of the CSCE mission that the people they spoke to that they had determined to have been there for two months or more were innocent civilians who had not borne arms against the Serbian captors, was that impression correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not know that. I did not keep a record as to how much time a person spent there. Two days, one month, two months, longer ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were civilians. That's indisputable [Realtime transcript read in error "That's I say disputable"]. But there were also soldiers in civilian clothing. Not all of them were wearing uniforms. Whether somebody was brought there as a military person or as a civilian, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you had no knowledge about who may have been soldiers or civilians who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I also understand that you had no knowledge about how they came there, how they arrived there, who had brought them, for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you check on a daily basis the amount of food the prisoners or those detained there received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there when lunch was served, breakfast and lunch, because we took our food at the same place, from the same cauldron. And they gave them the same rations as they gave me and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you stay there so that you could observe all of them receiving food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not observe. Food was distributed outside and all of them were outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "All of them," meaning how many exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said they were all outside when they received food. I asked you how many there were that you did observe receiving food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depended. It wasn't the same number every day. Some people would leave in the morning to go out to work. Not all of them would be on site. Because food was distributed at the workplace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether those who went outside received lunch or not, you wouldn't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know, but I judged that they did get food because they volunteered to go out to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do, Mr. MacDonald, if I could just to check with the witness here. Witness, you were asked a question whether -- at page 25, line 16, Judge Orie asked you a question: "And that there were civilians?" And you said: "They were civilians." That -- you are now recorded as having said: "That's I say disputable." I thought I'd heard something different. Did you say anything different? I thought I heard you say "indisputable."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said some of them were in civilian clothing and whether they had ever been on the front line, I don't know. Whether they had ever been in combat, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But at this specific point, did you say it was disputable that there were civilians or did you say that it was indisputable that there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's disputable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, you were aware that the Muslim detainees were suffering from violence inflicted on them by the guards, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. People said all sorts of things, but I never eye-witnessed that kind of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You know Predrag Bastah and Goran Viskovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: They were both guards at Susica camp when you worked there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a short while. They didn't stay there long as guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You're aware that they were both convicted before the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina for crimes committed in Susica and Vlasenica, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I know, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31640.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, this is the verdict in that case. The crimes that these two were found guilty included taking prisoners away from Susica, many of whom are still missing. And in particular, Goran Viskovic, a member the VRS, was found guilty of taking prisoners away to perform forced labour and for the rape of one of the female detainees. According to the verdict, the Susica guards were present while these crimes were taking place. You must have been aware at the time that these crimes were taking place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When did you find out about these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I found out after I left Susica, after the 26th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, but when?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I can't remember when. People talked around the town. How much of it was true, I don't know. I was not a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, when the witness says, "I was not there at the time," that suggests that he has received information about when it happened, and from your question, I think, it does not appear when it happened. So, therefore, that creates confusion. We have difficulties in assessing the reliability of the witness's evidence if we do not know what the date of the crimes charged are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: These crimes are charged between June and September 1992. And for clarity, you were working at Susica camp during that time, weren't you, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked at Susica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You worked in Susica between June and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, one of your former colleagues, a Muslim that had also provided security for TO material at Susica before the war, was also held at Susica camp, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31638. Your Honours, I'd ask that this not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Is there any instruction to be given to the witness in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, you'll see someone's name on the page in front of you. Please don't read that name out. He was a former colleague of yours at Susica, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't see that name on the screen. I do, I do. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Was that person a former colleague of yours at Susica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a neighbour of ours. His house is next to the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Did he work at the Susica with you before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He worked in the forestry company. He didn't work in the TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if we can have page 3 in the English of this document. I think it's also page 3 in the B/C/S. Yes, that's right. The paragraph at the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, you can read this paragraph, and you'll see this person states that you are firstly his friend and that he was working with you. Now, he was working with you, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: He never worked with me. No. He was just a neighbour to all of us guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can have page 7 in both documents -- both languages, my apologies. I'll move to the second-last paragraph in the English, and I believe it's the sixth-last paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Mr. Deuric, this person describes an incident where Dragan Nikolic pushed a gun into his mouth and then states that you came in the hangar and that you saved his life. Do you recall that incident, Mr. Deuric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that incident, nor did I see it. I gave the same evidence last time. I didn't see it. It's possible that it happened, but if they saw me as somebody they knew, they may have stopped doing it when they saw me and then that person understood that I saved his life. But I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, did you go into the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No. I came to the door. I think somebody had a visit, a visitor, and they were looking for a guard. If they couldn't find a guard, they would address me and ask: Could you go and get such and such, and then I would tell that person that he had a visitor. In such cases, I would go to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 31641.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is your testimony from last time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to move to page 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, of course, I do not know how we'll proceed. However, if you'd look at your question at page 29, line 16, then you see that that question contains two elements, and where the witness said that they never worked together, the emphasis and the focus was entirely on that element. The other element was lost which may be relevant and important. This is an encouragement also to avoid composite questions. Now please proceed where I stopped you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it's lines 6 to 12 here. And, Mr. Deuric, again, this is not in your language so I will read it out to you. The Prosecutor in that case is asking you about this incident, and he states: "So this is the big paragraph in this statement when this colleague of yours said that Nikolic was pushing gun to his throat and you entered the big, new building. Do you see that, Mr. Deuric?" You reply: "I see it. You were then asked: "So do you remember this?" And you reply: "I didn't see him put his rifle into his mouth, but I met Jenki on his way out of the warehouse." Firstly, Jenki was Dragan Nikolic's nickname, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deuric, I'd suggest to you that you do, in fact, remember this incident taking place, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that incident. I state that to you with full responsibility. I'm saying that that is possible that they had seen me, but I did not see them when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, could the witness tell us who "them" are? You said you didn't see "them." What you did refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Jenki and that friend of mine who said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you never see him or did you only not see him at the incident described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that situation, in that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- but you do know that he was in Susica although you do not remember to have seen him in those particular circumstances. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was in Susica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you -- and he was detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have an answer to the second element of your question earlier put to the witness, Mr. MacDonald. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, this Chamber has received evidence of other witnesses who were held in Susica camp. One testified that two prisoners were taken out sometime after lunch. He states he heard only screaming. Then the prisoners were brought back in, one of whom was unconscious. And he stated he overheard them saying they had been beaten by the A tower outside the hangar. The reference there is P207, paragraph 42. That A tower, that's the one you testified was 15 to 20 metres away from the door of your warehouse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Did you see or hear this beating taking place by that tower?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Didn't see it, didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The same witness stated he was able to see a patch of blood that had soaked into the sand by that A-shaped tower whenever he went to the toilet, and that is at paragraph 50. The witness who was a former colleague of yours, the one we've just discussed about the incident with Dragan Nikolic, he stated that whenever it rained, the rain would bring the blood bubbling back up at that A-shaped pole. And that is page 7 of 65 ter 31638 in both languages. Did you see this blood-soaked patch of sand by the A-shaped pole at any point when you were working at Susica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please now have P00193.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, this is a VRS security assessment from June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we have page 4 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That security assessment relates to Susica. I'm looking for the second-last paragraph in the English, the fourth-last paragraph in the B/C/S, where it states: "In order to prevent informing the public about the prisoners' appearance and the conditions they live in, any attempts to take recording devices and explosives inside or conduct interviews must be prevented, extensive movement must be prohibited and so on." Mr. Deuric, the VRS stated this -- recommended this measure because there were innocent civilians who had been detained for lengthy periods of time, who looked pale, thin and haggard, and had been subject to violence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: You know what? It's not that I was there and that I could be checking on everything that was going on. I had my own duties. I was not there non-stop, from morning to night. I had my time off too. I could go home, get some rest. I cannot know everything that was going on there within the compound, both when I was there and when I was not there. Even when I was within the compound, I had my own work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, I'm going to turn to my last topic which is the end of Susica as a camp. Towards the end of September, just before you heard the heavy gun-fire from Rogosija, there were just over 100 prisoners at Susica camp; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know how many there were because every day they went out and worked. It was only in the evening that everybody was within the compound. I was not there in the evening, so I could not assess how many there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- could I ask the witness a few questions. You said they went out for work but you didn't see them in the evening because you weren't there. Did you not see them returning to the camp in the early evening hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them in the morning in the camp when I would arrive from home, those who would line up and go out to work. And then that would happen on the following day as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I was asking about them returning in the evening hours to the camp, whether you saw them then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes. Sometimes when I would stay longer, I would be there within the compound when they would arrive. But if I would leave earlier, then they would not have been back. They would arrive only later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you usually have left already when they returned, or was it more common that you were still there, when they returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depended on the work. If I had more work to do at the warehouse, then I would stay on, and then they would come back by that time. If I had no work, then I went home early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there were situations where you -- why you had to stay later, but my question was whether usually - that is, during most of the days - you would have left already or whether most of the days you would still be there if they would return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, they would return while I was still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the question was whether there were 100 prisoners. Could you tell us -- you said: Well, I wouldn't know because I wasn't there in the evening, and you saw them in the morning. Why wouldn't you be able to tell that there were approximately 100 if you saw them in the morning hours and on many days also returning in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you, I wasn't the one who was supposed to count them so that I would know approximately how many of them there were there. It's possible that there were up to 100. I'm saying possible. Perhaps there were less. I'm not sure. I cannot talk about things that I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, an assessment of about 100, you can make that, isn't it? No one is asking you whether it was 95 or 105 but approximately a hundred. You'd know that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 07651C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, this is an excerpt from the war diary of Novica Simic, the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. And it's in the top right of the B/C/S and the bottom left of the English, you'll see a note stating: "Birac Brigade" and the date 20th -- or 20.09. I should say this war diary is from 1992. Now, you were still working at Susica camp on the 20th of September, 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And inside the box, it states: "Prison in Vlasenica. Women 2. Men 130." So does that aid your recollection in late September there were over 100 in the prison in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: According to what is written here, if that is correct, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: What I'm asking, Mr. Deuric, and I'll be as specific as possible, is whether this aids your recollection that there were 132 people in Susica on the 20th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution moves --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not understand what the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last answer, Witness, or the last thing you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution moves to tender this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document number 07651C receives number P6936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, this Court has heard evidence that the prisoners remaining in Susica were taken out and executed following a speech of Radovan Karadzic on 29 September and not, as you say you were told in your statement, taken for exchange. Apart from what you claim Dragan Nikolic said to you, do you know anything else about the fate of the detainees that were in Susica camp at the end of September?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't have any other knowledge. That is what I was told at the funeral on the 29th of September, when the funeral took place of my two nephews who were killed at Rogosija and also there were these two sons of my cousin. I was late for the funeral. As we were returning from the funeral I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, I'm asking about the fate of the people in Susica. Now, some of the people identified as last seen in Susica camp have subsequently been exhumed from mass graves including one in Ogradice. The people left in Susica camp at the end of September 1992, they were murdered, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination. There's one other matter, I forgot to tender excerpt 07021A. I'd seek to tender that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was an excerpt of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The CSCE mission to Susica camp, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that includes the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 07021A will receive number P6937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I remembered that one on my own. My colleagues have reminded me of a second, the verdict in the case against Predrag Bastah and Goran Viskovic. The verdict is quite long, Your Honours. I believe it is about 80 pages. I would seek to tender the first few, but I'm happy to discuss with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you just put to the witness that they were convicted. You gave the date of the charges and the type of charges, that was forced labour and a few things. The witness couldn't tell us anything further. What's the purpose of now tendering that? If there's no dispute those people having been charged and having been convicted and sentenced for those crimes, then what else would we -- are we supposed to learn from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The witness confirmed that the two people convicted were guards at Susica camp, Your Honours. There is some detail with regard to the crimes, and the Prosecution submits it is connected with his testimony about what took place and, in particular, the aspect of the -- the volume of crimes that took place at Susica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I -- I would like to leave it to you to first engage in a conversation with Mr. Stojanovic to try to find out before we get a judgement on our desk, which, of course, then we would have to study in detail, where not much more is said about than what we heard from the witness and from your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. Just for the record that's 65 ter 31640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification for the time being. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P6938.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Marked for identification. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deuric, just a few questions. Where did you get this knowledge that some of the people who were in Susica asked voluntarily to go out and work outside the Susica facility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what they said themselves, those people who went out to work. They said that they liked to go out and work. They'd go out a bit. It was mostly people like plumbers, masons, and other craftsmen. They went to work wherever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they say that to you personally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I would hear them saying that as they were talking amongst themselves and saying that to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question, were they paid for that work they performed? Witness, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know about, whether they were paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see at any point in time anyone who was in Susica not receiving one of the meals that was brought into Susica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything like that. I'm not sure of that. I didn't hear anyone say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Stojanovic please turn off his microphone when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to finish with the following question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're invited to switch off your microphone once the witness is answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to finish with the following question. Were you able to see whether medical staff visited the Susica facility at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had such an opportunity. Perhaps twice I saw medical staff coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deuric, on behalf of the Defence of General Mladic, I would like to thank you for the effort that you made, and we have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one question for you or more, I do not know yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To follow up on the last question of Mr. Stojanovic, what kind of medical staff arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I'm asking you. What kind of medical staff? Doctors, nurses? How many? You said "perhaps twice." Can you give us some more details.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I was present twice when they arrived. I think that some people complained of some stomach trouble. They examined them outside. There was a doctor. I didn't approach them. I don't know what the results were. A few of them were examined then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know? How do you know that a few were examined then by this doctor? You said you didn't approach them.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, I could see that, if I was 20 metres away or 30 metres away. I wouldn't approach them, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did the medical examination take place outside of a building? In the open?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: At the entrance into the building. In front of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was the doctor alone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were these two nurses there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means three people. And that happened twice.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I think twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many prisoners were examined by this doctor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You saw that, you told me just a minute ago, you could see that 20 metres away. How many patients? How many prisoners as patients were examined by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Well, several approached them. I didn't pay attention to count how many people were examined and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And how do you know why they were examined because of trouble with the stomach?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard from those -- those who were there, around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What kind of people were around?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Those who were there present in the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who were they? Guards, prisoners, staff, your colleagues? Who?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Guards and prisoners alike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And they told you what the reason for the medical examination was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: They were talking amongst themselves, and I know that two persons died in the compound. It's possible that's when the doctors came. I heard a medical panel established that they had died of natural causes because of cardiac problems. That was the talk that I heard. I wasn't interested. I had my own work to take care of. I also heard that there were some people who had stomach trouble. Whether it was the same panel, whether it was then that the doctors came, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two short questions on the same matter. Did you know the doctor? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he a local physician?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would have been a local physician, would you have known him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You knew the doctors of Vlasenica, the general practitioners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR DEURIC
utterances.text: Some I knew; others I didn't. I used to go to the health centre when I needed something. But they changed very often, and I didn't know all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. MacDonald?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the place for the videolink and for having answered all the questions that were put to you. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, at the other side of the videolink, we'll close the link, but apparently you do not hear me because you've not -- you don't have your earphones on. The videolink is closed. Just for the parties to know that where in the English the word "indisputable" was used when it was about the status of the detainees, that there is likely a mistake there which will be most likely corrected on the transcript. Just for your information. Then after the break, I'd like to start with reading a decision and then I think we'd continue with the cross-examination of the witness which we had to -- which had to wait since Thursday. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we will resume the -- to hear the evidence of witness, there are two matters which I would like to briefly deal with. First, it is about videolinks and it's primarily addressing the Defence at this moment. On the 18th of November of this year, the Chamber expressed its concern with recent videolink motions filed by the Defence which did not provide adequate evidence of the alleged inability or unwillingness of witnesses to travel to The Hague. In relation to the videolink motion filed on the 3rd of November, the Chamber notes again a lack of sufficient current supporting medical documentation. The Chamber therefore instructs the Defence to supplement the motion no later than the 28th of November, 2014, and the supplement should consist of a witness declaration relating to his position vis-à-vis travelling to The Hague and/or recent medical documentation substantiating the witness's inability to travel. The other matter deals with associated exhibits related to Vladimir Radojcic. The Chamber now takes this opportunity to deliver its decision on the tendering of associated exhibits with Witness Vladimir Radojcic. On the 2nd of July of this year, the Defence requested that it be permitted to make written submissions regarding the tendering of a large number of associated exhibits for Witness Radojcic. Pursuant to the Chamber's instructions of the 15th of July, the Defence filed its submissions on the 17th of July and tendered 51 associated exhibits. The Chamber notes that this represents a reduction, although limited, from the original number of 61 associated exhibits. On the 25th of July, the Prosecution filed a response, noting that the proposed associated exhibit bearing Rule 65 ter number 18618 had already been admitted into evidence as Exhibit P6617 and objecting to the admission of 14 of the 50 remaining associated exhibits predominantly on the basis that, and I quote: "These documents possess marginal relevance and are minimally probative, if at all, to material issues in this case." More specifically, the Prosecution is opposing the admission of 11 of these 14 tendered associated exhibits on the basis that they constitute inadmissible tu quoque evidence. The Prosecution further noted that for document bearing Rule 65 ter 1D2153, withdrawn as an associated exhibit by the Defence, a revised translation was made available to the Defence, which the Prosecution would like to tender, together with the original translation. The Chamber has reviewed the 14 proposed associated exhibits objected to by the Prosecution and understands that these documents are reports signed by Witness Radojcic, commander of the 1st Infantry Ilidza Brigade, to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Command, and largely relate to either combat activities in the witness's zone of responsibility and/or UNPROFOR activities in Sarajevo during the indictment period. In relation to whether 11 of the 14 exhibits constitute tu quoque evidence, the Chamber reminds the Prosecution of its oral decision of the 22nd of July, 2014, in which it advised the parties that, generally, the Chamber does not consider evidence to be tu quoque solely on the basis of its subject matter. This can be found at transcript page 24.510. The Chamber therefore finds that these 14 proposed associated exhibits are not deprived of relevance or probative value and, accordingly, will now address whether they, along with the other proposed associated exhibits tendered by the Defence, meet the admission criteria for associated exhibits. The Chamber recalls that the case law with regard to the admission of associated exhibits pursuant to Rules 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater establishes that documents can be admitted if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony.
