In order to satisfy this test, the tendering party must demonstrate that the witness's evidence, with references to the proposed associated exhibits, would be incomprehensible or of less probative value without the admission of those associated exhibits into evidence. The Chamber elaborated on its interpretation of the case law with regard to the admission of associated exhibits on the 9th of July, 2012, at transcript pages 530 to 531; in its written decision of the 23rd of July, 2012; on the 22nd of November, 2012, at transcript pages 5601 to 5603; and in its written decision of the 7th of February, 2013. Following this, the Chamber finds some of the underlying documents, once admitted into evidence, ensure that Witness Radojcic's evidence is not incomprehensible or of less probative value. The Chamber therefore hereby admits documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D2030, 1D2087, 1D2130, 1D2131, 1D2134, 1D2146, 1D2148, 1D2150 up to and including 1D2152, 1D2155 up to and including 1D2158, 1D2161, 1D2162, 1D2164 up to and including 1D2166, 1D2168, 1D2171, 1D2173, 1D2175, 1D2177, 1D2179, and 1D2180 into evidence as associated exhibits to the written statement of Witness Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there may be some confusion about one of the numbers I just mentioned, where the transcript at this moment reads twice 1D2162. I intended to say that the Chamber admitted 1D2161 and 1D2162 into evidence. Madam Registrar is invited to assign exhibit numbers by way of internal memorandum. The Chamber notes that in various instances the proposed associated exhibits referred to in the statement does not correspond with the comment made by Witness Radojcic in his statement. The Chamber finds that the remaining underlying documents do not form an inseparable and indispensable part of Witness Radojcic's written statement and consequently the Chamber hereby denies their admission into evidence without prejudice. With regard to document bearing 65 ter number 1D2153, the Chamber notes that it was withdrawn as an associated exhibit by the Defence and is now tendered by the Prosecution. The Chamber is wondering - and I'm asking the Defence - whether the Defence does object or does not object to the tendering of this document by the Prosecution. It was on your list, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, Witness Radojcic was led by my colleague Ivetic and he is not with us today, so if you can give us one or two days to consult with him. I really don't know from the top of my head now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whatever your position will be, according to the Prosecution, the Defence is also in receipt now of a revised translation of this document from CLSS. I take it that Mr. Ivetic will then also confirm that he has received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest that the Defence will upload that revised translation and inform the Registry about it, and that once this is done, that we'll decide on either MFI or admit the document tendered by the Prosecution although uploaded by the Defence into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber also notes that the original B/C/S versions of documents bearing 65 ter numbers 1D2149 and 1D2172 appear to be the same document although their translations differ, and the Chamber wonders whether the Defence could advise the Chamber which original and which translation is to be tendered and to do that no later than the 28th of November. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the request for admission of associated exhibits to Witness Radojcic's statement. Then, if the Defence is ready to call its next witness -- not to call its next witness, but to continue the -- that the witness be -- that the Defence witness will be escorted in the courtroom in order to allow the Prosecution to continue its cross-examination. Because that's where we are, as far as Mr. Barasin is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Barasin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had to wait for a while. Apologies for that. But we had a witness to be heard through videolink. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we please have 65 ter 1D02034.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, sir, one of the documents you discuss in your statement is Exhibit D676, an excerpt from the book: "To forget about a crime is also a crime." Did you read this book in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't read this book and I did not refer to it. I referred to the book called: "Cunning Strategy" by Sefer Halilovic. Although there are some similarities. I haven't read this book. I just leafed through it, but there are some similarities. The book I read is "Cunning Strategy" by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have perhaps paragraph 18 of the witness's statement on the screen, and that's D790. And, Your Honours, because it's just a brief reference by 65 ter number, perhaps -- I'll inquire only briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Here, at the end of paragraph 18, we see a reference to 65 ter 1D02034b which the Defence has informed us is an excerpt from the book we saw on our screen a moment ago. Is it your evidence now that you did not consider that book or review that book in preparing your statement?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this book. I said already I read "The Cunning Strategy" by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I noticed, Mr. Traldi, that we have a b number, whereas on the transcript you're quoted to have said "1D02034." We apparently have a b number here and when I try find to that b number I don't find it at this moment. And that's, of course, the Defence which should clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the list of associated exhibits provided by the Defence, it is a small a number instead of a small b number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you explain to us the reference to 65 ter 1D02034a in your list of associated exhibits and to the reference to the same number but then 1D02034b in the witness's statement. What did you show the witness? What was shown to him? And is -- are both uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that I received some kind of explanation from my case manager, and I have to check it with him again. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you check, Mr. Lukic, do note that the description of 65 ter 1D02034a is given as: "To forget about a crime is also a crime."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And a, as a matter of fact, is indeed an excerpt of that book in e-court. At least that's the title. And I think from what I understand from the B/C/S is that, indeed, the title gives a -- the word "zlocin," I think it is, twice, which makes me believe that the title in English is indeed the title as we find it in e-court in the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would definitely go with that title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, then, of course, that raises some issues because you are the one, Mr. Lukic, you are -- is reported as having interviewed the witness. Now what did you show him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He didn't read a book but I showed him some excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From this book?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From this book, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are telling us that you read another book. Was -- were excerpts of this book shown to you by the Defence? That is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence showed me excerpts but I didn't read the whole book. I just saw the introduction where he describes the establishment of the Patriotic League. I mean the authors of this book. And I saw some information about what happened in Sanski Most, the ethnic structure of the 1st Assembly in Sanski Most. I saw that but I haven't read the whole book, only excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And your comment is about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those parts of the book were shown to me by the Defence counsel. But I didn't see the book itself. Only the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have 65 ter 1D02034 back on our screens. I'll be looking for page 379 in the B/C/S only. This page has not yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to point II, the title of that section that we see in the table of contents is: "Serb aggression on Sanski Most"; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning to page 380, the next page, the next section we see as a title -- the title is: "Zlocini," which is "crimes"; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's written, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were you aware that this book discussed crimes which were committed against non-Serbs in many areas of Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this book. I just saw excerpts from it immediately before my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Under this section, we see references to crimes committed in several specific places. I'm going to ask you, first, about your time in the 1st Krajina Corps information service. At the time that you were serving in the 1st Krajina Corps information service, were you aware crimes had been committed against non-Serbs in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo as we see the second subsection under crimes?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in that part of the theatre at the time of the combat activity. That means in 1993. My activity was mainly in Posavina, Bosanski Samac, Modrica, et cetera. I wasn't in this part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you know today as you sit there, that crimes - including the massacres of about 25 unarmed Bosnian Muslims in Vrhpolje - occurred in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it from various articles and the testimony of some Bosniaks and politicians, but I never saw myself any documents, nor do I have any direct knowledge because I wasn't there in that area at the time. I know most of what I know from the media and from the excerpts of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page we see a list of locations, each of which start with "logor." Those are camps; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence of the camps that we see here during your time in the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about this camp and I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, are you aware that non-Serbs in Sanski Most were detained in, for instance, a camp called Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see, I didn't hear about this camp. However, the concept of camp in our language at the time of the past war was sometimes used when a group of people would travel and then spend some time in a particular area for a while. I don't think we had traditional camps. What happened in Manjaca at the beginning of the war could perhaps be called camp. Otherwise, there were no real camps. And in my understanding of the word "camp," I could hardly apply it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- you are giving quite general statements about the meaning of the word "camp," where you were asked whether you know anything about a camp at Betonirka. Now forget about the word "camp." Do you know of any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, if would you say that instead of commenting on what the word "camp" means, because whether a camp means A, B, or C, you don't know anything about Betonirka. So if you say there was no camp there, you wouldn't know because you don't know about what was there in Betonirka. So would you please refrain from giving these general statements and your conclusions about what a camp is and that there were no camps if you have no knowledge about what was there in Betonirka. Would you please keep that in mind. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, just to be completely clear, you don't have any idea whether the people in Betonirka or any of these facilities had simply "travelled and then spent some time there," because you don't know anything about these facilities; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of combat, I was never in that part of the theatre of war, and I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago that you didn't think that "we had traditional camps." Who did you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I understand you excluded Manjaca from that categorisation. Now the Chamber has received evidence about a number of other camps; for instance, Batkovic. Were you ever there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I heard about it, but I haven't been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Chamber has received evidence about camps operated in Prijedor municipality by the Bosnian Serbs, the police under the military. Were you ever at any of those camps?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once. It was called the collection camp in Trnopolje which held non-Serbs in some sort of free arrangement because, in Prijedor, at that time, there were attacks during those days against non-Serbs and the police organised that centre in order to be able to protect the non-Serb population from individual cases of violence. I know that it was an open-type facility where people could move around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a couple of follow-up questions on that as well. First, what month and what year were you there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. I think it was in July or August. I'm not quite sure about the month, but it was early in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you said -- I noticed you said in your evidence that the police had organised it. The Chamber has received evidence that the commander was a man named Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was a member of the Prijedor TO and then placed under the control of the Prijedor garrison of the VRS. So I'd put to you that you don't have any personal knowledge as to who organised the camp or who was responsible for it, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if my learned friend could be just more specific which facility. Maybe it's confusing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are talking about Trnopolje, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. Though I'm happy to restate the question more specifically if Mr. Lukic would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it is about Trnopolje, then we could read the question again. Whether you have any personal knowledge as to who organised Trnopolje camp or facility and who was responsible for it, do you have any personal knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not precisely but I know I had been there. There were members of the police and the army. I know Mr. Kuruzovic was in charge. But at the time both members of the army and the police acted jointly to enforce law and order in Prijedor. In peacekeeping in Prijedor. I was not there to inspect the camp, if I can add this. I was the guide for a group of foreign representatives who wanted to see the -- the camp. I worked at the press centre, and I escorted foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For how long were you in Trnopolje camp or in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One day, several hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "several hours"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I noticed in your last answer that you mentioned that members of both the police and the army were there and that you were aware Mr. Kuruzovic was in charge. In your first answer, you mentioned only the police. Now, are you aware that General Mladic is charged, among other things, with crimes that took place against non-Serb civilians in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, nobody was harmed or killed in Trnopolje. That's the information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether you are aware that Mr. Mladic is charged with, among other things, crimes that took place against non-Serb civilians in Trnopolje camp. So whether he was charged with that. Whether it happened or not is a different matter. Are you aware with him being charged with such crimes committed in Trnopolje? I see you're nodding yes. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand. I didn't understand the question at first. I did not know he was charged in connection with that camp as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we left off on Thursday discussing "Krajiski Vojnik" and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you move on to another one. Do I understand your testimony well that people were free to go to Trnopolje and went there on their own free will? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it was presented both to me and to the foreign reporters. The people who were there provided that information to me and the foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The people who are there are who exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand but at the camp you have prisoners, you have the management of the camp. Did Mr. Kuruzovic say something about it or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. It was said to the journalists and that was confirmed by the people there, that they were not prisoners of war, nor were they brought there by force. They were instead brought there to be protected from the violence that could happen to them in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the only source of knowledge you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But again you said: "It was said to the journalists and it was confirmed by the people there ..." Which people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm talking about the people who spoke to me and the foreign journalists. The non-Serbs who were there in Trnopolje. It was the yard of a schoolhouse. There were no other attributes of a traditional camp. It was just an area protected by the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Exactly in relation to police and army, this question was put to you. Who provided you with this information? Who else -- were they the police and army members or the people who were held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told by people who worked as security in the camp and the people who stayed at the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a slightly different question on the same subject, sir. You indicated that these people were there voluntarily and they were free to move in and out as they pleased; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you were there for the two and a half hours, did you observe any people moving in and out freely of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And if you allow me, Your Honours, I would like to add one more thing. The people to whom I spoke to at the camp were talking to me without the presence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you add on what you want to add. You say -- I just want to understand exactly what you said. You saw these people moving in and out of the camp and going away for good and nobody stopping them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They went in and out. I don't know within which period of time, but I know they were going in and out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "I don't know within which period of time," what do you mean exactly by that? It's not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman asked me if they would leave permanently. I don't know if they would go away and not come back because any stay there long enough. But I was able to see that they could go out and come back freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you say "the gentleman," you're referring to the media that you guided around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I mean the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say you saw them leaving but whether they would stay out for a longer period of time or a shorter period of time, you wouldn't know. How far could you see them? I mean, they were walking out or they were driving out? What did you see? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They walked out. There were no vehicles anywhere around, and I did not observe their further movement. Because it was not the purpose of my visit to observe them. It was to talk to these people. And I also wanted to tell you, Your Honours, that while we spoke to the non-Serb people in the camp, there were no guards or anyone else present who could tamper with our conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they carrying any luggage when they moved out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you could follow them at what distance? 100 metres, 200 metres? Did you follow them in any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they moved in all directions. I didn't look particularly. It wasn't the purpose of my visit, but I could see they were going out and going in all directions. And some people were going out. Others were coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Going out and in what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a yard, the yard of a school, and it had a fence around it. They slept in the schoolhouse, those who spent one or more days there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say you saw them leaving the yard of the schoolhouse which was fenced in. And you saw them coming back within that fence without any further details about how long they went away, how far they went away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why they went away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber has received evidence, documents from the 1st Krajina Corps - and I'll refer, for instance, to P2875 and P3708 - that referred to arrested people being placed in Trnopolje and referred to it as a prison camp. Now, with the exception of two and a half hours that you spent there with foreign journalists, you have no knowledge of the conditions there; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: With that, I will turn back to "Krajiski Vojnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could 65 ter 11822 be brought to our screen. Now, this is another article published in "Krajiski Vojnik," and again, it's an interview with President Karadzic. If we could turn to page 5 in the English and in the B/C/S, the far right of the image on the screen, just before the last bolded question, we read: "Let me say this also. This leadership thinks that we should unite with Serbia, not Yugoslavia. We think that it is necessary for Krajina to unite with us. What is being done at present is because of the international environment. First steps will be made in direction where there is the least resistance. No one can stop our unification with Serbia, and then with God's help, when Serbia breaks out to Una, it will be much easier for Krajina to fulfil its goal."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, again, we have "Krajiski Vojnik" publishing an interview with President Karadzic where he is advocating unification with Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Krajiski Vojnik" took over this interview from a different newspaper "Glas Srpska." That is to say, this is not part of our own editorial work. This was just taken from another paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Una there is a reference to the Una river; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 11822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 11822 receives number P6939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 05927 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While that comes up, like the 1st Krajina Corps, the VRS Main Staff had a sector for legal, moral, and religious affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That sector was under General Gvero; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head of this organ in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. General Gvero was the head of this organ in the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Main Staff sector for legal, moral, and religious affairs published a magazine called "Srpska Vojska"; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was "Srpska Vojska" distributed to 1 KK units like "Krajiski Vojnik"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the single paper of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an article by General Gvero for "Srpska Vojska" called: "Silk cord for Alija." Are you familiar with this article?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, looking at the third paragraph in both languages, General Gvero is giving his position on the cause of the war. And he says: "The Serbs had to fight or disappear ..." And then says: "It was a question of fighting or assent by the survivors to the (now) vengeful, sinister Asiatic, Turkish oppression and constant threats by Ustasha knives and in Ustasha pits." Now, this rhetoric as published in "Srpska Vojska" is being distributed throughout the 1st Krajina Corps units; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the words "that they would be killed," who added that? Is that interpretation by anyone? It seems not to be a linguistical explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm told that it's been added by the translators of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not in the original document. It's just an interpretive remark which is not based purely on language but on apparent understanding of the translators of what those threats would be about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And the slashes are intended to indicate, as I understand it, to the reader that it is an interpretive step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But why do we find that before us? Why is it not removed? I mean, we have had the issue about what "balija" means or what "Turks" means, now we have got an interpretation. But I think that it doesn't fall within the scope of those explanations, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're happy to have it revised, if the Chamber prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not only that, but it shouldn't have been there. That's the first thing that -- unless there's a better explanation than you've given until now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll ask a couple of follow-up questions about that language, actually. What does the term "Ustasha knives" refer to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a historical dimension of this interpretation. It pertains to the Second World War when many Serbs were killed by the Ustasha knife. That is the symbol of the suffering of Serbs in Jasenovac and other Ustasha camps during the Second World War. What I have to say here primarily pertains to the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where an enormous number of Serbs were killed in Ustasha camps mostly but also during the offensive at Mount Kozara. So that is this historical memory of the suffering of the Serb people in the First and Second World Wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how do you understand "Ustasha pits"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the Second World War, a large number of Serbs were killed in the Karst regions where there are these natural pits, abysses. I don't know how to explain this. Serbs were thrown into these pits alive and would die in them. That happened a great deal in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct, then, that both the references to "Ustasha knives" and to "Ustasha pits" in your understanding refer to ways in which Serbs had been killed?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This text here actually reminds us of this historic dimension of this suffering and it is a plea for it not happen again, not to have this kind of genocide repeated or this kind of suffering repeated. This struggle was supposed to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the term "Turkish" used above, just above the word "Ustasha," that's used in Bosnia as a derogatory term for Bosnian Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. That's not right. When it says here "the vengeful, sinister Asiatic, Turkish oppression," that is the Ottoman occupation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when children were taken, Serb children, and then trained to become Janissaries. So this is a reminder of the Ottoman rule in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, there was no Ottoman army or Ottoman presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 when this article was published, was there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're right. That was not there then. But what is stated here is that this struggle, this war that started in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, in some of its manifestations and forms is reminiscent of that period of Ottoman rule. So that is the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I put to you that it's clear that when General Gvero suggests there's a risk of Turkish oppression, he is clearly not speaking of Bosnia being reconquered by Turkey, he is clearly speaking of the potential of a Bosnian Muslim government in some of these areas. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have a few more questions on this document. I see that we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom and we'll take a break of 20 minutes, and we'll resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 of this document in the English, in the second paragraph, and the fifth paragraph of the document in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, looking at the second sentence, we read -- I'm only interested in the first part of the sentence for the moment: "The Croats and Muslims in these parts, former Serbs ..." "Srpska Vojska" published the suggestion that Bosnian Muslims and Croats were former Serbs who had been converted; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's not that they were converted of their own will. This was done forcibly. They were forcibly converted to Islam, for instance, during the Ottoman rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One term used for people like that is "poturice"; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes such a term is used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's commonly understood as a derogatory term, right, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. Because Serbs were forcibly converted to Islam or to Catholicism. This process went on during this war as well, from 1991 to 1995. In order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Later in this paragraph, we read about Muslims and Croats: "Extreme uncivilised, often savage behaviour towards Serb and their fanatic hatred of the Serbs, a hatred so strong that it is aimed at the extermination of Serbs by all methods and most often the most bestial ones." This is propaganda; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree that it's propaganda only. Because I have to remind you, if Their Honours allow me, that already at the end of the 1980s there was this anti-Serb hysteria that started and demands for the breakup of Yugoslavia. The beginning of the war in Croatia and the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was precisely marked with this attack on the Serb population. I dealt with these crimes in the film "Genocide," and in a way this led to fear instilled among the Serb people that World Wars I and II would be repeated. And then there was this defence to prevent this genocide or these genocides.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You said this led to a fear. Also to anger; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not anger. Not rage. There is historical memory that is still alive. Let me tell you, my father took part in the previous war and then I took part in this one, so practically every generation is forced to wage war. And then there is this fear of constant clashes among peoples and ethnic groups, and this led not to rage but to calls for organising the people in order to prevent what had already happened in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say: "There is historical memory that's still alive." These are vivid and painful historical memories; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And General Gvero is calling them to mind clearly in this article; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he is reminding people of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The people he's reminding are all of the soldiers in 1st Krajina Corps units to whom this was distributed, right? Among others?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would "Srpska Vojska" also have been distributed to the units in the other VRS corps?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the paper of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it was distributed to all troops of Republika Srpska throughout the territory of Republika Srpska. It was only "Krajiski Vojnik" that was distributed only within the 1st Krajina Corps. That was our very own paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the article's title: "A silk cord for Alija," is a reference to what General Gvero describes as a medieval assassination technique for Turkish leaders; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. He used the metaphor here; namely that Alija's policy would lead to that. That was the train of thought of General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 05927 as the next public Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05927 receives number P6940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, could you also give us a time indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask for P2874 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document, it was put to you that the Serbs asked to be separated from the other two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the 21st of May, 1992. In the 1st Corps, in your 1st Corps, in the territory where it was deployed and from where it was manned, at that time, had war operations already started?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of May ...

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. Yes, there were combat operations in the territory of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you come across documentation from 1991 about the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, for instance?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see some documents, some information. The process of the establishment of Herceg-Bosna started already in June 1991 when the top people from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the Croat community there, met with Tudjman in Zagreb. And then other meetings follow --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the meetings at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was the 8th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, because you're speaking so fast --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you please resume from where you said: "And then other meetings follow ..." Could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the meeting between the Croat leaders from Bosnia-Herzegovina and Franjo Tudjman in June 1991, a number of other meetings followed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of them is the conference in Grude which resulted in the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, in April 1992. That is what was proclaimed in public by the Croat leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that in this way they wished to round off the historic borders of the Croatian people. That is to say, together with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do not see this here. What did you say, what was the intention? What, with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To have part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Croats live, as they say, that's where they're historically live, they want to unite in a joint state, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I heard that, unite, but it was not reflected in the record, so that's why I asked you once again. And the objective, the creation of the HVO and the Croatian Herceg-Bosna what was the objective? Was it to separate from the other two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of everything I've seen and heard, that was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this 21st of May, 1992, do you know, did you receive any information in the course of your work that there were attacks against facilities of the JNA, members of the JNA, even before the Army of Republika Srpska was established?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you mean 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1992. Already when the war started in Croatia in 1991, but intensively in the second half of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, there were intensive attacks against the members of the JNA and the facilities of the JNA. I have to remind you after this meeting on the 28th of February in Mehurici - those were the Muslim leaders - they proclaimed that this illegal Patriotic League was established at the time. And at that moment it had nine regional staffs for Bosnia-Herzegovina, 103 municipal staffs, and they also had this staff for Sandzak, that is to say, Serbia and Montenegro, that is to say, the territory where the Muslim population lived. And in that proclamation they said that they already have about 120.000 persons that they can put in the function of war. As for the defence of the Muslim people, there was this directive -- I mean, that was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then in that directive they expressed their plan as to how the Muslim population would be moved out in planned fashion, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in parts of its territory. Likewise, instructions were provided for attacks against JNA facilities and attempts would be made to prevent them from leaving the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mean, let me just add another thing in that sense. There were these well-known attacks against the Tuzla column in May and the attack in Sarajevo in Dobrovoljacka Street. These are just drastic examples. There were many attacks in Western Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the members of the Patriotic League, the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. That's what it said there. Truth to tell, later on, when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established out of the Patriotic League, then there were also members of other ethnicities there. But, of course, a small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anything was offered to the Muslims to stay on living with the Serbs in a rump Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And, likewise, what was sought was not to have this well-known referendum take place, the one that was held on the 1st of March in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Serbs did not take part in that, but the call was that we should live together in a joint state, in one state. However, this anti-Serb hysteria that started in the 1980s, it continued, and the Badinter Commission ruled as it did and the referendum was held against the will of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Belgrade Initiative?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't exactly say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What about the Skopje Agreement? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Skopje Agreement was concluded in the first half of May, I cannot remember the exact date. And this was the agreement between Blagoje Adzic, the then chief of General Staff of the JNA, and President Alija Izetbegovic. And it implied the peaceful withdrawal of JNA units from Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, this agreement failed already when Alija Izetbegovic returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina, when this well-known attack against members of the JNA took place as they were withdrawing from Dobrovoljacka. So, in fact, the agreement was rejected in that way by the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were Serbs in favour of a status quo or were they in favour of some changes?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We or, rather, the Serbs then advocated talks and seeking a common solution. It was repeated many times that it was better to negotiate for years than wage war for a few days. I think that this was a constant call to the Muslim side and the Croat side to sit at the negotiating table and try to prevent a war. No one had forecast a war but what was constantly being said that it was much better to negotiate than to wage war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now mentally go back to Trnopolje briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I encourage you to ask questions which arise from cross-examination. That's the first one. And, second -- and moving to Trnopolje, there's a fair chance that you will. And, second, that you ask questions about matters which are in dispute, because I wasn't aware that there was any dispute about the Green Berets being a predominantly or exclusively Muslim organisation, but I may have missed the position of the Prosecution that it was a multi-ethnic organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was proposed by the Prosecution that that was Serbs who wanted separation from another two nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- Mr. Lukic, I'm just -- the last example was about the Green Berets being Muslim. Is there any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was to show who was for the separation. Exactly. It is in blunt contradiction with what the Prosecution claims, trying to establish through this witness. And I think that we have full right to challenge it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Apparently you disagree with my observations. You will have another couple of minutes. Mr. Traldi, as matters stand now, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Certainly not much. Probably none at all, but I'll evaluate over the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, Witness, that you saw a fence in Trnopolje. Did it go all around the building and how tall it was?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was up to an average man's chest. It was the existing fence of the school. It was not built especially for the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who you said were going out and going off in all directions and coming back, did they go out escorted by guards or on their own, and did they come back escorted by the guards or alone?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any escorts. I saw people coming out -- going out and coming back but without any escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court P6940.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Gvero, did his job include propaganda?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge of these matters in any army, including combat activities, has to cover propaganda because war includes propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document, General Gvero says: "Everybody knows that Serbs did not want this war, that they did everything to avoid it." To the best of your knowledge, is this propaganda or fact?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not call this propaganda. I think it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was put to you that there was the Ottoman yoke and atrocities and the constant threat of Ustashas, killing fields and knives, but in the third paragraph of this document, we read: "However, in this war, which they did not want, which was imposed on them, the Serbs had no choice. They had to fight or disappear." To the best of your knowledge, was this war imposed on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I maintain and believe that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I participated in that war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just -- I don't think it affects the answer necessarily, but just for the record, I don't recall putting to the witness that there was the Ottoman yoke in 1993. And I'd like my questions accurately reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see whether the witness can finish his answer and then let's move on. It's on the record, Mr. Traldi. Please proceed. You may finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the war was imposed on the Serbs. And I know, as one of the participants, that nobody ever told me we needed that war. We were all placed in a situation where we will to understand and accept that the war was imposed on us, and we had to protect the people from the same things happening to them as earlier in our history. And from all I know, I conclude that this war was imposed on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, on page 1 of this document, and it's probably page 2 in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 in English. [In English] We have to move to the third one obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second full paragraph in English: "From the beginning of this war, the Serbs have been proposing to stop it. The Muslims proclaimed war. Serbs propose peace and negotiations for peace. The Muslims carry out new ever-large -- larger-scale offensives." In your view, is this propaganda or fact?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are facts. And by the way, Mr. Cutileiro confirmed it in a 1995 interview, that peace had already been concluded when Alija reneged on it. That peace plan, the Cutileiro Peace Plan had been accepted by all sides to the war but then Alija Izetbegovic unilaterally rejected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this is in dispute between the parties. I'll ask you because I believe no evidence has been led on the subject. What was it that the Serbs feared? How many Serbs were killed in World War II?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 1.700.000. That's the figure I know. Around 700.000 were killed in Jasenovac camp alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barasin. We extended a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just a couple, Mr. President. I'd need less than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm looking at the interpreter's booth, whether less than five minutes -- and it's not my promise but it's Mr. Traldi's promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have a problem if everybody else can stay longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi, not more than five minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't personally participate in any peace negotiations between the Republika Srpska authorities and the Bosnian government, did you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, you did not; or yes, you did?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me: "Right?" And I said no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, for instance, the Chamber has received evidence that the Cutileiro Plan was never signed by the Bosnian Serbs. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Even then it was presented in the public that the plan had been accepted, and I also read an interview by Mr. Cutileiro who said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question is whether it was signed. If you say that Mr. Traldi is wrong that it was not signed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not signed by any of the parties at the time. It was accepted but only initialled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That completes my questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's less than five minutes, Mr. Traldi. I think the interpreters can have more trust in you than they would have in me. Witness, this concludes your testimony. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and also for having the patience to stay over the weekend and to wait this morning until the other witness has finished his testimony. I thank you for having answered all the questions that you were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 25th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of November, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.21 p.m.,
